title: Using COM Components
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of using com components in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Introduction to Component Object Model (COM) and Creating COM objects.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study using com components as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 81 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Using COM Components matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP often relies on Windows COM components and external services for file operations, messaging, XML, and integration. For 'Using COM Components', document the exact component/provider version, permissions, bitness, network boundaries, timeouts, and recovery behavior. Never construct a filesystem path or external URL directly from untrusted input, and keep secrets outside the public web root and repository.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Introduction to Component Object Model (COM); Creating COM objects; Using object properties and methods; Component registration; Component permissions; 32-bit and 64-bit compatibility; Identifying third-party component dependencies. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Using COM Components
content_blocks.code:
<%
Dim component
Set component = Server.CreateObject("Scripting.Dictionary")
component.Add "state", "ready"
Response.Write Server.HTMLEncode(component("state"))
Set component = Nothing
%>
content_blocks.run_instructions: This system COM component illustrates activation only. Vendor components require their own registration, permissions, dependency, and bitness checks. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use approved test data and a component/service you control. Confirm path permissions, host allow-lists, timeouts, malformed responses, and cleanup behavior. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of using com components. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of using com components using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Introduction to Component Object Model (COM). State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

summary: Using COM Components is one step in the larger Classic ASP request, state, data, security, or maintenance workflow.

The syllabus coverage includes Introduction to Component Object Model (COM); Creating COM objects; Using object properties and methods; Component registration; Component permissions; 32-bit and 64-bit compatibility; Identifying third-party component dependencies.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
